complexity.notes: The approach is convoluted and non-idiomatic: sorting values then reverse-lookup by linear scan is O(k*u) and fragile; collections.Counter plus heapq.nlargest(k, counter, key=counter.get) or counter.most_common(k) would be clearer and directly satisfy the better-than-O(n log n) follow-up. Also, the final set(output) dedupe both masks the duplicate-inclusion issue and discards deterministic ordering.
complexity.space: O(min(n, 20001)) for the frequency map and output
complexity.summary: Counts frequencies in a dict, sorts the frequency values, takes the k largest, then re-scans the map to collect every key matching those frequencies and dedupes via a set. Correctness that exactly k elements are returned relies on the problem's guaranteed uniqueness of the answer (no tie at the k/(k+1) frequency boundary).
complexity.time_average: O(n + u log u + k*u), where u is the number of unique elements; with the stated constraint that nums[i] is in [-10^4, 10^4], u <= 20001 so this simplifies to O(n)
complexity.time_worst: O(n^2), since adversarial hash collisions degrade the n dict insertions/lookups to O(n) each
